blocks.text: **Varicella zoster virus (VZV)** is a herpesvirus that targets both **skin and nerves**. The primary infection is **chickenpox**, usually caught in childhood by **aerosol or direct contact**, and it is very contagious to anyone who is not immune. Children usually have a mild illness; **adults, pregnant women and the immunocompromised** are hit much harder.

blocks.title: Chickenpox at a glance
rows: K&C and KC Essentials 14–21 days; First Aid 10–20 days
From up to 4 days (usually about 48 h) before the rash until the **last vesicle has crusted**
KC Essentials: from 2 days before; First Aid: from 24 h before
Where the rash starts and spreads
Often mucosae first, then **centripetal**: heaviest on the trunk, sparse on the limbs
K&C: face, scalp and trunk, fewer on the extremities
Pink macule → vesicle → pustule within about 24 h; a **new crop every 2–4 days**, each with a spike of fever

blocks.text: Because lesions erupt in **crops**, one patch of skin shows **every stage at once**: macules, papules, vesicles and crusts side by side. The lesions itch, and mucous membranes are involved. Fever stops once new crops stop appearing.

blocks.title: Complications
items: **Secondary bacterial skin infection** from scratching: the **commonest** complication.

**Varicella pneumonitis**: mainly adults, pregnancy and the immunocompromised; **smokers** are at extra risk. It starts 1–6 days after the rash, the chest X-ray shows diffuse changes in both lungs, and it can kill.
Other visceral disease in high-risk groups: hepatitis, encephalitis; disseminated multi-organ infection in the immunocompromised.
CNS disease is rare (about 1 in 1000 cases in K&C) and is classically a self-limiting **acute truncal cerebellar ataxia**.

blocks.title: Chickenpox in pregnancy and the newborn
rows: About **3%** risk of fetal damage affecting the eyes, CNS and limbs (Davidson). K&C quotes 1–2% embryopathy if infection is in the first 20 weeks.
**Severe neonatal varicella** with visceral involvement and bleeding
Higher risk of severe chickenpox, including pneumonitis

blocks.text: The books disagree on chickenpox numbers. Davidson gives incubation **11–20 days**, infectivity from **up to 4 days** before the rash, and a **3%** fetal risk in early pregnancy. K&C gives 14–21 days and 1–2%. Use Davidson’s figures, but whichever book you use, infectivity ends only when **all lesions have crusted**.

blocks.note: Look at: panel A, a generalised vesicular rash with the trunk most affected (chickenpox); panel B, a rash confined to one thoracic dermatome (shingles).

blocks.text: Diagnosis is **clinical**. If confirmation is needed, test fluid aspirated from a vesicle by **PCR for VZV DNA** or by **direct immunofluorescence** for antigen. **VZV IgG serology** is mainly used to find **seronegative (susceptible)** people after an exposure.

blocks.title: Who gets an antiviral for chickenpox?
rows: Usually **none**: treatment shortens the rash by only about 1 day
Treat if seen within **24–48 h** of the vesicles appearing: oral aciclovir **800 mg five times daily**, famciclovir 500 mg three times daily or valaciclovir 1 g three times daily, for **5 days**
Treat whatever the timing. Start with **IV aciclovir 5 mg/kg three times daily**, switch to oral once improving, and continue until **all lesions are crusting**

blocks.text: The antiviral window differs: Davidson treats adults seen within **24–48 h** of vesicle onset; KC Essentials says over-16s seen within 48 h; K&C allows over-16s up to 72 h. Use Davidson’s window. **Immunocompromised and pregnant patients are treated regardless of timing.**

blocks.title: VZ immunoglobulin (VZIG) after exposure: all three criteria are needed
items: **Significant contact**: e.g. sharing a room for 15 minutes or more, face-to-face contact, or a hospital contact with a case.
**Susceptible**: no history of chickenpox or shingles, ideally confirmed by a **negative VZV IgG**.

**Predisposed to severe disease**: immunosuppression (disease, transplant, recent chemotherapy, or high-dose steroids within the last 3 months), **pregnancy at any stage**, newborns of mothers with peripartum chickenpox, or premature babies born before 28 weeks.
Timing: ideally within **7 days** of exposure, but it may still soften the illness up to **10 days**.
If severe chickenpox develops despite VZIG, treat with **aciclovir**.

blocks.text: A **newborn** qualifies for VZIG when the mother’s chickenpox starts no more than **5 days before or 2 days after delivery**, because the baby is at risk of severe neonatal varicella.

The **live attenuated varicella vaccine** is given as **two doses**: one after the age of 1 year and a second at 4–6 years. Seronegative adults get two doses at least a month apart. The UK does **not** use it routinely: it is offered mainly to **health-care staff who lack immunity** and to people **living with an immunocompromised person**. First Aid adds that it can be given to people with HIV whose CD4 count is above 200.
A hospital patient with suspected chickenpox needs **airborne plus contact** isolation while the work-up is under way.

After chickenpox, VZV lies **latent in dorsal root and cranial nerve ganglia**. **Reactivation** produces shingles, most often in **older people**, and only in someone who has had chickenpox before. Fluid from shingles vesicles can give **chickenpox** to a non-immune contact, but chickenpox never causes shingles in a contact. Zoster is less contagious than chickenpox.

blocks.title: Clinical features
items: **Burning pain or tingling** in one dermatome comes first; grouped vesicles on a red base appear about **3–4 days later**, confined to that dermatome on one side.
**Thoracic** dermatomes are the commonest site; the **ophthalmic division of the trigeminal nerve** is also often affected.
A brief viraemia can produce a few distant “satellite” chickenpox-like spots.
**Zoster sine herpete**: dermatomal paraesthesia or pain with no rash.

blocks.text: **Severe, prolonged, multi-dermatomal or recurrent** zoster suggests underlying immune deficiency, **including HIV**. Herpes zoster is in the **CD4 < 500** risk band. Step-Up adds: zoster in someone **under 50** should make you think of immunosuppression.

blocks.title: Special sites and complications
rows: Corneal vesicles can ulcerate and cause **blindness**, so arrange **urgent ophthalmology** review. K&C: about 50% get eye complications, cut to 20% or less by early aciclovir.
**Facial palsy**, loss of taste on the same side, and vesicles in the **external ear canal**; VIII nerve involvement adds vertigo and sensorineural deafness. Easily mistaken for **Bell’s palsy**.
Cranial nerve palsy, myelitis, encephalitis; **granulomatous cerebral angiitis** causing a stroke-like illness, especially after ophthalmic zoster
The **commonest** complication; more likely with **older age** and a more intense initial rash

blocks.text: Davidson describes PHN as pain persisting for **1–6 months or longer** after the rash has healed. K&C (neurology) and First Aid define it as pain lasting **more than 4 months**. K&C says it affects about 10% of patients, mostly elderly, responds poorly to analgesics and tends to ease over about 2 years.

blocks.title: Treatment and prevention
rows: Same drugs and doses as chickenpox (aciclovir, valaciclovir, famciclovir) but usually for **7–10 days**; start oral therapy within **72 h** of the rash (K&C)
Treat **every** case however mild; give **parenteral** therapy
Reduces acute and later pain, especially in the **over-65s**, and reduces eye complications in V1 zoster
**Amitriptyline** 25–100 mg daily, **gabapentin** (from 300 mg daily), **pregabalin** (from 75 mg twice daily), **capsaicin 0.075%** cream
Live attenuated and recombinant zoster vaccines reduce shingles and PHN; offered to adults over **70 (UK)** or over **60 (USA)**

blocks.note: Look at: a one-sided band of grouped vesicles that stays within a single dermatome, typical of shingles.

blocks.text: **Infectious mononucleosis (IM, glandular fever)** is a syndrome of **pharyngitis, cervical lymphadenopathy, fever and lymphocytosis**. It is usually caused by **Epstein–Barr virus (EBV)**, a gamma herpesvirus passed in **saliva** (in adolescents and adults, often by kissing). The same picture can come from **CMV, HHV-6/7, primary HIV-1 infection and toxoplasmosis**. EBV is not very contagious, so cases do not need isolation.

blocks.title: Clinical features
items: Severe sore throat, often with **tonsillar exudate**; enlarged **anterior and posterior cervical nodes** (non-tender in Davidson).
**Palatal petechiae**, **periorbital oedema**, **splenomegaly** (about half of patients), sometimes a macular or petechial rash.
Fever usually settles within about 2 weeks; fatigue takes a few more weeks.
Age matters: mild and short in **under-10s**; severe and prolonged in **over-30s**, often without a sore throat (may present with jaundice or prolonged fever).

blocks.title: Complications (Davidson)
rows: **Rash after ampicillin (80–90%)**, hepatitis (80%), prolonged fatigue (10%), jaundice (<10%), severe pharyngeal oedema
Neurological (cranial nerve palsies, polyneuritis, transverse myelitis, meningoencephalitis); haemolytic anaemia, thrombocytopenia; myocarditis, pericarditis; interstitial nephritis
**Splenic rupture**, **airway obstruction**, agranulocytosis, X-linked lymphoproliferative syndrome

blocks.title: Investigations
rows: **Atypical lymphocytes**, which are **activated CD8+ T cells**. First Aid: the lymphocytosis itself is mostly B-cell proliferation.
Positive in about **90%** from the **second week** (K&C). It may be negative early, so **repeat** it; many children and about 10% of adolescents never become positive.
Acute infection: **VCA IgM** and antibody to early antigen, with **anti-EBNA absent**. Anti-EBNA appears about 1 month later (KC Essentials: 6–12 weeks).
Mild thrombocytopenia; mildly raised transaminases, ALP and bilirubin
Looks for secondary β-haemolytic streptococcus (about 30% carry group A strep)

blocks.text: **Atypical lymphocytes are not specific to EBV.** They also occur with CMV, acute HIV, viral hepatitis, mumps, rubella, **dengue and malaria**. The heterophile test can be **falsely positive** in viral hepatitis, Hodgkin lymphoma and acute leukaemia (KC Essentials adds SLE and HIV).

blocks.title: Management
items: **Supportive**: rest, fluids, paracetamol or NSAIDs. Current antivirals do **not** work against EBV.
If throat culture grows β-haemolytic strep, give **penicillin**. **Avoid ampicillin and amoxicillin**, which commonly cause an itchy rash.

**Glucocorticoids only for complications**: severe pharyngeal or tonsillar swelling threatening the airway (Davidson: prednisolone 30 mg daily for 5 days), neurological involvement, or marked thrombocytopenia or haemolysis.
**No contact sport until splenomegaly has resolved**: splenic rupture is a risk in the first few weeks and can present with left shoulder-tip pain.
Return to work or school depends on how well the patient feels, not on blood tests. About 10% develop a chronic relapsing illness.

blocks.title: Long-term EBV associations
items: **Endemic Burkitt lymphoma** (falciparum malaria areas of Africa), **nasopharyngeal carcinoma**, some Hodgkin lymphomas, primary CNS lymphoma, post-transplant lymphoproliferative disorder.
**Oral hairy leucoplakia** in AIDS.
**X-linked lymphoproliferative (Duncan’s) syndrome**: boys with an SAP gene mutation cannot control primary EBV infection.
**Haemophagocytic lymphohistiocytosis (HLH)**: fever, rash, jaundice, hepatosplenomegaly, nodes, **cytopenias and a very high ferritin**, with haemophagocytosis in the marrow; mortality is high.

blocks.note: Look at: panel A, atypical (reactive) lymphocytes on a blood film; panel B, the widespread rash after ampicillin in IM.

blocks.text: CMV is a herpesvirus that **stays for life**, latent in cells of the monocyte/macrophage lineage (K&C), with intermittent silent shedding in **saliva, urine, semen and genital secretions**. A second wave of infection affects young adults, peaking at **25–35 years**, through sexual and oral spread. Over half of adults are seropositive (K&C).

blocks.title: CMV disease depends on the host
rows: Mostly silent. Some get an **IM-like** or prolonged flu-like illness. Compared with EBV: **hepatomegaly more common**; nodes, splenomegaly and pharyngitis less common. **Heterophile negative.**

Primary infection in pregnancy: about **40%** pass it to the fetus. Petechiae, hepatosplenomegaly, jaundice; about **10%** have long-term CNS damage (microcephaly, **cerebral calcification**, chorioretinitis, **deafness**). K&C: the **commonest congenital infection** (0.3–1% of births)

blocks.text: **CMV retinitis**: **painless**, progressive loss of vision in severe immunosuppression. On fundoscopy the **vitreous is clear**, with retinal **haemorrhages and exudates** and sheathed vessels (“**frosted branch angiitis**”; First Aid calls it “pizza pie”). Ganciclovir or valganciclovir **halts progression, but lost vision does not return**. Mimics include toxoplasmosis (vitritis, no haemorrhages) and HIV retinopathy (cotton wool spots).

blocks.title: Diagnosis
items: Healthy host: **CMV IgM** plus a fourfold IgG rise or seroconversion; heterophile test negative; atypical lymphocytosis less marked than in EBV; **ALP raised out of proportion to transaminases**.
Immunocompromised host: antibody tests are unreliable, so show CMV **in the affected organ** (PCR, antigen, culture or histology).
Most infections are now diagnosed by **quantitative PCR** for CMV DNA or RNA.
Histology: enlarged cells with intranuclear **“owl’s eye” inclusions**.
Blood CMV is useful in **transplant** patients but correlates poorly with disease in **HIV**; urine CMV helps only in **neonates**, because shedding continues lifelong.

blocks.title: Treatment
rows: **Ganciclovir 5 mg/kg IV twice daily** or **oral valganciclovir 900 mg twice daily** for at least 14 days
Long-term maintenance unless ART restores immunity

blocks.text: Ganciclovir commonly causes **bone marrow suppression**, works less well for CMV **pneumonitis**, and resistance can emerge on long-term therapy.
CD4 threshold: Davidson places CMV disease in the **CD4 < 100** band; First Aid quotes **< 50**. Use Davidson’s figure.

blocks.note: Look at: an enlarged infected cell with a large intranuclear “owl’s eye” inclusion, the histological hallmark of CMV.

blocks.text: Dengue is a **flavivirus** with **4 serotypes**, spread mainly by the **day-biting _Aedes aegypti_** mosquito, which breeds in standing water. Infection gives **lifelong immunity to that serotype** but only a few months’ protection against the others. It is the leading cause of fever in travellers returning from **South/South-east Asia, Latin America and the Caribbean**.

**Why the second infection is the dangerous one:** dengue haemorrhagic fever (DHF) and dengue shock syndrome (DSS) follow infection with a **different serotype**. Existing antibody increases viral uptake into cells bearing **Fc receptors** and drives T-cell activation and cytokine release, causing **capillary leak and DIC**.

blocks.title: Clinical course
rows: About 2 days of malaise and headache
Abrupt fever, headache, **pain on eye movement (retro-orbital)**, backache, severe aches (“**break-bone fever**”), scleral injection, **relative bradycardia**, lymphadenopathy
Continuous or **saddle-back**: a dip on day 4–5, then a second rise; lasts about 7–8 days
Blanching maculopapular rash from **days 3–5**, spreading out from the trunk and **sparing palms and soles**, often as the fever falls
**Days 3–7** after fever onset: plasma leak can lead to DHF or DSS

blocks.title: WHO 2015 case definitions
rows: Fever in someone exposed where dengue is endemic, plus **at least two** of: aches and pains, rash, nausea or vomiting, leucopenia, a positive tourniquet test, or any warning sign

Abdominal pain or tenderness, **persistent vomiting**, fluid accumulation (effusion, ascites), **mucosal bleeding**, **hepatomegaly > 2 cm**, **rising haematocrit with falling platelets**. These need medical intervention, e.g. IV fluids.

Severe plasma leak (shock, or fluid with respiratory distress), severe bleeding, or severe organ involvement (**AST/ALT ≥ 1000 U/L**, impaired consciousness, cardiomyopathy, AKI). These need emergency and intensive care.

blocks.title: Investigations
items: FBC: **leucopenia, neutropenia, thrombocytopenia**; **raised ALT/AST**. A **rising haematocrit** signals plasma leak.
**Tourniquet test**: inflate a BP cuff between systolic and diastolic for 5 minutes; petechiae below it reflect capillary fragility and low platelets, but the test is non-specific.
Early illness: **PCR for dengue RNA** or **NS1 antigen** ELISA (NS1 is less sensitive than PCR).

Later: **IgM seroconversion or a fourfold IgG rise**; KC Essentials advises taking serology from about day 5. Antibodies **cross-react** with other flaviviruses (yellow fever, Japanese encephalitis, West Nile).

blocks.title: Management and prevention
items: **Supportive only**: careful fluid replacement and treatment of shock and organ failure, with blood products if needed. With intensive care, mortality is **1% or less**.
**Avoid aspirin** (bleeding risk). **Glucocorticoids and antivirals do not help.**
Prevention: destroy breeding sites, use insecticides and repellents. Bed nets help little because _Aedes_ bites **by day**.
K&C: the licensed live tetravalent vaccine may **increase** the risk of severe dengue in people who have never been infected (seronegative).

blocks.text: Telling the _Aedes_-borne viruses apart: **chikungunya** → prominent joint pain; **Zika** → conjunctivitis, Guillain–Barré syndrome, fetal microcephaly; **dengue** → bone pain, bleeding and shock.
A febrile traveller from a malaria area has **malaria until proven otherwise**, even if dengue seems likely; one negative blood film does not exclude it.
K&C’s classic description of dengue shock syndrome quotes mortality **up to 44%**; Davidson gives **1% or less** with modern intensive care. Early fluid management is what makes the difference.

blocks.note: Look at: the timeline of viraemia, fever, shock and bleeding, and which test (virus detection, PCR, antigen ELISA, IgM/IgG) works on which day of illness.

cards.back: Secondary bacterial skin infection from scratching the itchy lesions

cards.front: Who is at particular risk of varicella pneumonitis?
cards.back: Adults (especially **smokers**), pregnant women and the immunocompromised; it starts 1–6 days after the rash

cards.front: Three criteria that must all be met before giving VZIG?
cards.back: 1. Significant contact; 2. susceptible (no history, VZV IgG negative); 3. predisposed to severe disease (immunosuppressed, pregnant, at-risk newborn). Give ideally within 7 days, up to 10 days.

cards.front: Chickenpox treatment in a pregnant or immunocompromised patient?
cards.back: IV aciclovir 5 mg/kg three times daily, then oral until all lesions crust, regardless of how long the rash has been present

cards.front: Ramsay Hunt syndrome: which ganglion and which features?
cards.back: Geniculate ganglion: facial palsy, same-side taste loss, vesicles in the external ear canal
Amitriptyline, gabapentin, pregabalin, or capsaicin 0.075% cream
Severe disease, prolonged rash, several dermatomes involved, or recurrence

cards.front: EBV serology pattern in acute infection?
cards.back: VCA IgM and anti-early antigen present; **anti-EBNA absent** (appears about 1 month later)

cards.front: What are the atypical lymphocytes in infectious mononucleosis?

cards.back: Painless visual loss; clear vitreous; retinal haemorrhages and exudates with vessel sheathing (“frosted branch angiitis”)

cards.front: First-line treatment of CMV disease in the immunocompromised?
cards.back: Ganciclovir 5 mg/kg IV twice daily or valganciclovir 900 mg orally twice daily for at least 14 days; foscarnet or cidofovir if resistant or intolerant
Abdominal pain, persistent vomiting, fluid accumulation, mucosal bleeding, hepatomegaly > 2 cm, rising haematocrit with falling platelets

cards.front: Why is a second dengue infection more dangerous?
cards.back: Antibody from the first serotype boosts viral entry via Fc receptors and drives cytokine release, causing capillary leak and DIC (DHF/DSS)

questions.stem: A 27-year-old heavy smoker (about a pack daily) developed an itchy vesicular rash 3 days ago. He is now short of breath with a dry cough. His respiratory rate is 30/min and oxygen saturation 89% on air. Chest examination is unremarkable, but his chest X-ray shows widespread nodular shadowing in both lungs.
questions.leadIn: What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation: An adult **smoker** with chickenpox who becomes breathless within a week of the rash, with symptoms out of proportion to the signs and **diffuse bilateral** X-ray changes, has **varicella pneumonitis**. It typically starts 1–6 days after the rash and can be fatal.
whyNot: Lobar pneumonia gives focal consolidation, not diffuse bilateral changes, and does not explain the timing after the rash.
PE does not cause widespread nodular shadowing, and the link to the rash would be missed.
PCP occurs in advanced immunosuppression; nothing suggests that here, and the trigger is clearly the chickenpox.
Asthma causes wheeze and a clear chest X-ray, not bilateral shadowing.

questions.stem: A 5-year-old girl has had a fever and an itchy rash for 3 days. The spots are mostly on her trunk and scalp, with a few on her limbs and some in her mouth.
questions.leadIn: Which examination finding most strongly supports chickenpox?
options: Lesions at different stages side by side in one area
A rash concentrated on the palms and soles
Target lesions with a dusky centre
A rash that appears only as the fever settles
questions.explanation: Chickenpox lesions appear in **crops** every few days, so one patch of skin shows **macules, papules, vesicles and crusts together**. The trunk-heavy (centripetal) spread with mouth lesions fits too.
whyNot: Chickenpox is densest on the trunk and sparse on the limbs; a palm-and-sole rash points elsewhere.
A single-dermatome eruption is shingles (reactivation), not primary chickenpox.
Target lesions suggest erythema multiforme.
A rash appearing as the fever falls is typical of exanthem subitum (HHV-6/7). In chickenpox each new crop comes with fever.

questions.stem: A 29-year-old woman who is 20 weeks pregnant spent an afternoon with her nephew 4 days ago; he developed chickenpox the next day. She has never had chickenpox, and her VZV IgG is negative. She is well with no rash.
questions.leadIn: What is the most appropriate management?
options: Start oral aciclovir as prophylaxis for 5 days
Reassure her that no action is needed
questions.explanation: She meets **all three VZIG criteria**: significant contact, susceptibility (IgG negative) and a predisposition to severe disease (**pregnancy at any stage**). She is within the ideal **7-day** window. If chickenpox still develops, she should then be treated with aciclovir.
whyNot: In Davidson and K&C, aciclovir is given if chickenpox develops; the post-exposure step for a susceptible pregnant woman is VZIG.
The live vaccine is not used to protect a pregnant contact; VZIG is the post-exposure measure for her.
She is susceptible and at risk of severe maternal disease and fetal damage, so doing nothing is wrong.
Waiting for repeat serology wastes the window in which VZIG works.

questions.stem: A previously healthy 35-year-old man noticed the first chickenpox vesicles 18 hours ago. He feels unwell with fever but has no breathlessness, and his chest is clear. He is not immunosuppressed.
questions.leadIn: What is the most appropriate treatment?
options: Oral aciclovir 800 mg five times daily for 5 days
Symptomatic care only, with no antiviral
IV aciclovir 10 mg/kg three times daily for 14–21 days
Oral aciclovir 200 mg five times daily for 5 days
questions.explanation: An **adult** seen within **24–48 h** of vesicle onset should receive an antiviral: **oral aciclovir 800 mg five times daily for 5 days** (or valaciclovir or famciclovir).
whyNot: Withholding antivirals is reasonable in healthy children, but adults seen early benefit from treatment.
This high-dose IV regimen is for severe complications such as encephalitis or disseminated infection.
VZIG is post-exposure prophylaxis for susceptible high-risk contacts, not treatment of established disease.
200 mg five times daily is an HSV dose; chickenpox needs 800 mg five times daily.

questions.stem: A 72-year-old woman has had burning pain around the left side of her lower chest for 3 days. This morning a band of grouped vesicles on a red base appeared in the same area, stopping at the midline. She is otherwise well and not immunosuppressed.
questions.leadIn: What is the most appropriate treatment?
options: Oral valaciclovir 1 g three times daily for 7 days
No treatment; it will settle on its own
questions.explanation: This is **thoracic shingles** seen within **72 h** of the rash. A **systemic antiviral** at chickenpox doses for **7–10 days** reduces acute pain and the risk of post-herpetic neuralgia, especially in the over-65s.
whyNot: Steroids alone do not treat the virus and have not been shown to prevent PHN.
Topical treatment does not reach the infected nerve; a systemic antiviral is needed.
Gabapentin treats established PHN; it does not replace early antiviral therapy.
At 72 she is at high risk of PHN, and early antivirals reduce it.

questions.stem: A 66-year-old man has a painful vesicular rash over his right forehead and upper eyelid. His right eye is red and gritty, and he reports blurred vision.
questions.leadIn: What is the most important next step, alongside an oral antiviral?
options: Topical steroid eye drops started in primary care
Reassurance and review if the vision worsens
questions.explanation: Zoster of the **ophthalmic division (V1)** can put vesicles on the cornea, leading to ulceration and **blindness**. It needs **urgent ophthalmology** review as well as early antiviral therapy, which cuts eye complications.
whyNot: Steroid drops without specialist assessment are unsafe when the cornea may be infected.
A delay of weeks risks permanent visual loss.
This is a viral infection; an antibiotic is only for secondary bacterial infection.
Waiting for the vision to worsen risks irreversible damage; review must be urgent.

questions.stem: A 19-year-old student has had a sore throat and fever for a week, with enlarged posterior cervical nodes. Her GP prescribed amoxicillin for presumed tonsillitis. Two days later she developed an intensely itchy, widespread maculopapular rash.
questions.leadIn: What is the most likely underlying diagnosis?
questions.explanation: Sore throat, fever and **posterior cervical nodes** in a young adult suggest **EBV infectious mononucleosis**. An itchy rash after **ampicillin or amoxicillin** occurs in most patients with IM (80–90%), so these drugs are avoided.
whyNot: An itchy rash appearing after amoxicillin in a young adult with posterior nodes is the classic IM trap, not scarlet fever.
Measles is not triggered by an antibiotic, and the posterior nodes with sore throat fit IM.
Primary HIV can mimic IM, but the classic amoxicillin-rash link is with EBV.
Secondary syphilis does not present as acute tonsillitis with an antibiotic-triggered rash.

questions.stem: A 17-year-old boy has fever, exudative tonsillitis and splenomegaly. His Monospot test is negative on day 5 of illness. EBV serology shows a positive viral capsid antigen (VCA) IgM and a negative antibody to EBV nuclear antigen (anti-EBNA).
questions.leadIn: What does this serology indicate?
options: Past EBV infection with lifelong immunity
A false-positive result caused by lymphoma
questions.explanation: VCA IgM with **no anti-EBNA** means **acute primary infection**: anti-EBNA appears only about a month or more after the illness. The early negative Monospot does not exclude IM; heterophile antibody often appears only in the second week.
whyNot: Past infection shows anti-EBNA (and VCA IgG) without VCA IgM.
A positive VCA IgM shows that EBV infection is present.
In reactivation, anti-EBNA from the earlier infection would already be present.
False positives are a recognised problem with the heterophile test, not with this specific serology pattern in a classic clinical picture.

questions.stem: A 45-year-old man with untreated HIV (CD4 count 40 cells/mm3) notices painless, gradually worsening blurred vision in his left eye over 2 weeks. Fundoscopy shows a clear vitreous, with retinal haemorrhages and white exudates along sheathed vessels.
questions.leadIn: What is the most likely diagnosis?
options: Progressive outer retinal necrosis from VZV
questions.explanation: **Painless** progressive visual loss with a **clear vitreous**, **haemorrhages and exudates** and vessel sheathing (“frosted branch angiitis”) at a very low CD4 count is **CMV retinitis**.
whyNot: Toxoplasmosis typically causes vitritis (a hazy vitreous) and retinitis without retinal haemorrhages.
HIV retinopathy causes cotton wool spots and does not threaten sight.
Angle-closure glaucoma is painful, with a red eye and raised pressure, not retinal haemorrhages.
VZV outer retinal necrosis is a mimic, but it progresses rapidly; this is the classic CMV picture.

questions.stem: A 28-year-old nursery worker has had fever and fatigue for 3 weeks. She has a palpable liver but only a mild sore throat and no significant lymphadenopathy. Two Monospot tests are negative. Her ALP is markedly raised and her transaminases are only mildly raised.
questions.leadIn: What is the most likely cause?
questions.explanation: A **heterophile-negative** IM-like illness with **hepatomegaly**, few nodes and little pharyngitis, plus an **ALP raised out of proportion to transaminases**, points to **CMV**. Young adults (often those caring for small children) are a typical group.
whyNot: EBV usually causes marked pharyngitis and nodes, and a positive heterophile test by this stage.
Hepatitis A causes a hepatitic picture with high transaminases, not a predominantly raised ALP.
Strep tonsillitis would cause prominent pharyngitis, not a prolonged illness with hepatomegaly.
Toxoplasmosis can cause a heterophile-negative IM-like illness, but the hepatomegaly with a disproportionately raised ALP fits CMV best.

questions.stem: A 30-year-old woman returned from Thailand 5 days ago. She has a high fever, pain behind the eyes on eye movement, severe back and muscle pain, and a flushed face. WBC is 2.6 × 10⁹/L, platelets 90 × 10⁹/L and ALT 140 U/L. Three malaria blood films are negative.
questions.leadIn: What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation: Fever after travel to **South-east Asia** with **retro-orbital pain**, severe “break-bone” aches, **leucopenia, thrombocytopenia and raised ALT** is classic **dengue**. Repeated negative films make malaria much less likely.
whyNot: Malaria must always be excluded, but three negative films make it unlikely here.
Typhoid is in the differential for travellers from Asia, but retro-orbital pain, severe aches, leucopenia and low platelets after a short incubation fit dengue best.
Chikungunya is dominated by joint pain rather than bone and eye pain with low platelets.
Zika is usually milder, with conjunctivitis.

questions.stem: A 24-year-old man with dengue is on day 5 of his illness. His fever has just fallen, but he now has abdominal pain and persistent vomiting. His haematocrit has risen from 42% to 50%, and his platelet count has fallen from 80 to 35 × 10⁹/L. BP is 110/70 mmHg.
questions.leadIn: What is the most appropriate next step?
options: Admit for IV fluids and close monitoring
Discharge with oral fluids and review in a week
Oral aspirin for the abdominal pain
questions.explanation: He is in the **critical phase** (days 3–7) and has **warning signs**: abdominal pain, persistent vomiting and a **rising haematocrit with falling platelets**, which signal plasma leak. Warning signs need **medical intervention such as IV fluids** and monitoring for shock.
whyNot: Warning signs mean he must not be sent home; deterioration to shock can be rapid.
Glucocorticoids have not been shown to help in dengue.
Aspirin must be avoided in dengue because of the bleeding risk.
No existing antiviral works against dengue.

questions.stem: A 34-year-old man has painful vesicles spanning three adjacent thoracic dermatomes on the right. The rash has lasted 3 weeks. He had a similar episode on the left 6 months ago. He has lost weight recently.
questions.leadIn: Which investigation is most important?
questions.explanation: Step 1: recognise **shingles** (dermatomal vesicles). Step 2: notice the warning features: **young age**, **several dermatomes**, a **prolonged** rash and **recurrence**. Step 3: Davidson says these suggest **underlying immune deficiency, including HIV**, and herpes zoster sits in the CD4 < 500 risk band. Weight loss adds to the suspicion. So the key test is an **HIV test**.
whyNot: A chest X-ray does not explain recurrent, extensive zoster.
VZV IgG will be positive in anyone who has had chickenpox and adds nothing here.
There are no meningitic or encephalitic features to justify a lumbar puncture.
The Monospot test is for EBV infectious mononucleosis.

questions.stem: A 17-year-old rugby player has confirmed EBV infectious mononucleosis. His fever has settled and he feels better, but his spleen is still palpable. He asks when he can play again; there is a match next week.
questions.leadIn: What is the best advice?
options: Avoid contact sport until the splenomegaly has resolved
He can play now that the fever has settled
He can play once the Monospot test turns negative
A course of prednisolone will allow him to play sooner
He can play if he wears protective padding
questions.explanation: Step 1: the danger in IM is **splenic rupture**, which is most likely in the first few weeks. Step 2: his spleen is **still enlarged**. Step 3: Davidson says return to normal activity depends on how he feels, not on lab tests, but **contact sport must wait until the splenomegaly has resolved**. Step-Up suggests at least 3–4 weeks from symptom onset.
whyNot: Feeling well does not remove the risk of rupture while the spleen is enlarged.
Heterophile antibody can stay positive for months and does not guide return to sport.
Steroids are for complications such as airway obstruction, not for speeding return to sport.
Padding does not protect an enlarged spleen from rupture.

questions.stem: A 25-year-old nurse from the Philippines had dengue fever as a child. She now has dengue again and on day 5 develops hypotension, a rising haematocrit, pleural effusions and bleeding gums.
questions.leadIn: What best explains why this second episode is so severe?
options: Pre-existing antibody to a different serotype increasing viral uptake via Fc receptors
Loss of the lifelong immunity to the serotype she had as a child
Direct viral destruction of the bone marrow
An immune-complex glomerulonephritis causing fluid overload
questions.explanation: Step 1: the picture is **dengue shock syndrome**, with capillary leak (raised haematocrit, effusions, hypotension) and bleeding. Step 2: DHF/DSS happen when someone immune to **one serotype** is infected by **another**. Step 3: the existing, non-protective antibody **increases viral entry into Fc-receptor-bearing cells** and drives T-cell activation and cytokine release, causing **capillary leak and DIC**.
whyNot: Immunity to the original serotype is lifelong; the problem is that cross-protection against other serotypes lasts only months.
Thrombocytopenia occurs, but the shock is from plasma leak, not marrow destruction.
Nothing here suggests malaria; the mechanism is immune enhancement.
The fluid shift is from capillary leak, not kidney disease.

questions.theme: Viral syndromes in adults and newborns
questions.leadIn: Match each patient below to the single most likely diagnosis in the list. Any option can be the answer for one case, several cases or none.

items.stem: A newborn has a petechial rash, jaundice and hepatosplenomegaly. A cranial scan shows periventricular calcification, and a hearing screen is abnormal. The mother had a flu-like illness in mid-pregnancy.
items.explanation: Petechiae, jaundice and hepatosplenomegaly with **periventricular calcification** and **deafness** are classic **congenital CMV**, the commonest congenital infection.

items.stem: A 45-year-old man has had pain in his right ear for 2 days. Today he cannot close his right eye or raise his right eyebrow, food tastes odd on the right of his tongue, and there are vesicles in his right ear canal.
items.explanation: A facial palsy with **vesicles in the external ear canal** and same-side taste loss is **Ramsay Hunt syndrome** (VZV in the geniculate ganglion), often mistaken for Bell’s palsy.

items.stem: A 23-year-old returned from Bali 9 days ago. On day 6 of her fever, the temperature has just fallen, but she is cold and clammy with BP 80/50 mmHg, a right pleural effusion and a haematocrit that has risen sharply.
items.explanation: Fever falling on days 3–7 (the **critical phase**) with **shock, an effusion and a rising haematocrit** means severe plasma leak: **dengue shock syndrome**.

items.stem: A 20-year-old had confirmed glandular fever 2 weeks ago. He now has persistent high fever, jaundice, hepatosplenomegaly, pancytopenia and a ferritin of 15 000 µg/L. A bone marrow aspirate shows macrophages engulfing blood cells.
items.explanation: Two steps: recent **EBV** infection, then fever, cytopenias, a **very high ferritin** and **haemophagocytosis** in the marrow. This is secondary **HLH** triggered by EBV, which has a high mortality.

questions.stem: A 4-year-old boy has chickenpox. His mother asks when he can go back to nursery without being infectious to others.
questions.leadIn: When does he stop being infectious?
options: When all of his lesions have crusted over
As soon as his fever settles
Exactly 5 days after the rash appeared, whatever the lesions look like
When no new spots have appeared for 12 hours
questions.explanation: Chickenpox is infectious from before the rash appears until **the last vesicles have crusted over**. All the sources agree on this end-point.
whyNot: Fever settles when new crops stop, but uncrusted vesicles are still infectious.
Antivirals do not make a child non-infectious within 24 hours.
A fixed number of days is not the rule; the end-point is crusting of every lesion.
Lesions that appeared recently will still be uncrusted vesicles.

questions.stem: A blood film from a 20-year-old with fever, sore throat and cervical lymphadenopathy shows many large atypical lymphocytes.
questions.leadIn: What are these atypical cells?
questions.explanation: The atypical mononuclear cells of IM are **activated CD8+ T cells** reacting to EBV-infected B cells. First Aid notes that the lymphocytosis is mostly B-cell proliferation, but the atypical cells seen are T cells.
whyNot: EBV infects B cells, but the large atypical cells on the film are reactive T cells, not malignant cells.
Reed–Sternberg cells are seen in Hodgkin lymphoma tissue, not on the blood film in IM.
They are lymphocytes, not monocytes, despite the name “mononucleosis”.
Plasma cells are not the atypical cells of IM.

questions.stem: A 26-year-old woman develops a primary CMV infection, confirmed by seroconversion, at 16 weeks of pregnancy.
questions.leadIn: According to Davidson, what is the approximate chance that the virus passes to the fetus?
questions.explanation: Primary CMV infection in pregnancy carries about a **40%** risk of fetal transmission. About **10%** of infected infants have long-term CNS problems such as microcephaly, cerebral calcification, chorioretinitis and deafness.
whyNot: 0.3–1% is the rate of congenital CMV across **all births**, not the risk after a primary maternal infection.
10% is the proportion of infected infants with long-term CNS sequelae, not the transmission rate.
Too high; transmission occurs in under half of cases.
Transmission is not universal; most fetuses escape infection.

questions.stem: A 32-year-old man returned from Vietnam 3 days ago with an abrupt fever, headache and retro-orbital pain that began yesterday. Malaria films are negative.
questions.leadIn: Which test is most sensitive for confirming dengue at this stage?
options: Dengue IgG on a single sample
questions.explanation: In the first days of illness the virus is in the blood, so **PCR for dengue RNA** (or NS1 antigen) is used; serology turns positive later (from about day 5). Davidson notes NS1 ELISA is **less sensitive than PCR**.
whyNot: IgG on one sample cannot show recent infection; serology needs IgM seroconversion or a fourfold IgG rise, and is negative this early.
NS1 is useful early and widely available, but it is less sensitive than PCR.
The tourniquet test is a non-specific bedside sign of capillary fragility, not a confirmatory test.
Paul–Bunnell detects heterophile antibody in EBV infection.

questions.theme: Choosing the right test in viral infections
questions.leadIn: Match each scenario below to the most appropriate investigation in the list. Any option can be the answer for one case, several cases or none.
options: EBV VCA IgM and anti-EBNA serology
PCR of vitreous fluid for CMV DNA
Dengue RNA PCR or NS1 antigen
Thick and thin blood films for malaria

items.stem: A 19-year-old has had a sore throat, fever and enlarged posterior cervical nodes for 10 days, and his spleen tip is palpable. A screening test is needed.
items.explanation: By the **second week** of a typical illness, the heterophile antibody (**Monospot**/Paul–Bunnell) test is a quick screen and positive in about 90%.

items.stem: A 16-year-old has fever, exudative tonsillitis and atypical lymphocytes. Two Monospot tests 10 days apart are negative. Her doctor wants to confirm or exclude EBV.
items.explanation: Many children and about 10% of adolescents never make heterophile antibody. **EBV-specific serology** settles it: VCA IgM with absent anti-EBNA means acute infection.

items.stem: A pregnant nurse is exposed to a child with chickenpox. She cannot remember whether she had chickenpox herself.
items.explanation: To decide on VZIG, first establish **susceptibility**: a negative **VZV IgG** confirms she is seronegative.

items.stem: A kidney transplant recipient 6 weeks after surgery has fever, leucopenia and mildly raised transaminases. The team suspects CMV disease and wants a blood test to detect the virus.
items.explanation: In **transplant** recipients, detecting CMV in **blood** is useful (unlike in HIV, where blood CMV correlates poorly with disease). Antibody tests are unreliable in the immunocompromised, and urine CMV helps only in neonates.

items.stem: A 27-year-old returned from Kenya 10 days ago with fever, headache and aching joints. Dengue is in the differential diagnosis.
items.explanation: Two steps: sub-Saharan Africa means **malaria dominates** the causes of fever in travellers, and any febrile traveller from a malaria area has malaria until proven otherwise. **Blood films** come first.

questions.stem: A 31-year-old woman who is 10 weeks pregnant develops chickenpox. She asks about the risk to her baby.
questions.leadIn: According to Davidson, what is the approximate risk of fetal damage?
questions.explanation: Maternal chickenpox in **early pregnancy** carries about a **3%** risk of fetal damage (eye, CNS and limb abnormalities) in Davidson. K&C gives 1–2% in the first 20 weeks. 40% is the transmission risk for primary CMV, which is a different question.
whyNot: This underestimates the risk; Davidson quotes about 3%.
Far too high for varicella embryopathy.
40% is the fetal transmission rate for primary CMV in pregnancy, not the varicella damage risk.
Far too high; most babies are unaffected.

questions.stem: A 74-year-old man had shingles in a left thoracic dermatome 5 months ago. The rash has healed, but he still has burning pain in the same area, and the touch of his shirt is unbearable.
questions.leadIn: Which drug is most appropriate now?
options: A repeat 7-day course of oral aciclovir
questions.explanation: Pain persisting after the rash heals is **post-herpetic neuralgia**. Davidson lists **amitriptyline**, gabapentin, pregabalin and capsaicin cream; amitriptyline is the only one offered here.
whyNot: Antivirals help when started early in the acute attack; they do not treat established PHN.
Steroids have not been shown to reduce PHN.
There is no active viral infection needing IV treatment.
The virus is no longer replicating in the skin; topical antivirals have no role in PHN.

questions.stem: A 20-year-old woman has confirmed EBV infectious mononucleosis.
questions.leadIn: Which additional finding would most clearly justify a short course of glucocorticoids?
options: Tonsillar swelling causing stridor and difficulty breathing
ALT three times the upper limit of normal
questions.explanation: Steroids are reserved for **complications**: **airway-threatening tonsillar or pharyngeal swelling**, neurological involvement, or marked thrombocytopenia or haemolysis. Davidson suggests prednisolone 30 mg daily for 5 days for severe pharyngeal oedema.
whyNot: Fever is part of the illness and usually settles within about 2 weeks; it is not a steroid indication.
Splenomegaly is managed by avoiding contact sports, not with steroids.
Mild hepatitis is common (about 80%) and does not need steroids.
Post-viral fatigue is common and is managed supportively.

questions.stem: A 52-year-old liver transplant recipient on tacrolimus has 2 weeks of bloody diarrhoea and abdominal pain. Colonic biopsies show enlarged cells with intranuclear “owl’s eye” inclusions.
questions.leadIn: What is the most appropriate first-line treatment?
questions.explanation: Owl’s eye inclusions confirm **CMV colitis** in an immunocompromised host. First-line treatment is **ganciclovir 5 mg/kg IV twice daily** (or oral valganciclovir) for at least 14 days.
whyNot: Aciclovir is for HSV and VZV; it is not standard CMV therapy.
Foscarnet is reserved for ganciclovir resistance or intolerance.
Mesalazine treats ulcerative colitis; the biopsy shows a viral cause.
Metronidazole treats anaerobic or C. difficile infection, not CMV.

questions.stem: A 28-year-old woman has probable dengue on day 4 of her illness. She is reviewed in the clinic.
questions.leadIn: Which finding is a WHO warning sign that needs medical intervention?
options: Liver palpable 3 cm below the costal margin
Pain behind the eyes on eye movement
A blanching rash that spares the palms and soles
A pulse rate lower than expected for her fever
questions.explanation: **Hepatomegaly > 2 cm** is one of the WHO 2015 **warning signs**, together with abdominal pain, persistent vomiting, fluid accumulation, mucosal bleeding and a rising haematocrit with falling platelets.
whyNot: Retro-orbital pain is a typical feature of uncomplicated dengue.
This is the typical dengue rash, not a warning sign.
Relative bradycardia is a recognised feature of ordinary dengue.
Leucopenia is one of the criteria for probable dengue, not a warning sign.

questions.stem: A 58-year-old man has a 2-day history of right earache. Today he cannot close his right eye and his mouth droops on the right. Taste on the right of his tongue is altered, and there are small vesicles in his right external ear canal.
questions.leadIn: What is the most important treatment?
options: An oral antiviral such as aciclovir
Prednisolone alone, as for Bell’s palsy
Reassurance; this will settle without treatment
questions.explanation: Facial palsy, same-side taste loss and **vesicles in the ear canal** mean **Ramsay Hunt syndrome**: VZV reactivation in the geniculate ganglion. K&C says shingles involving motor nerves such as the facial nerve is treated with **aciclovir**.
whyNot: Treating this as Bell’s palsy misses the VZV cause; the antiviral is the key treatment.
This is viral, not a bacterial infection.
The facial palsy is a significant complication needing active treatment.
The ear vesicles are viral; antibiotic drops do not treat VZV.

questions.stem: A 38-year-old man with HIV (CD4 count 60 cells/mm3) has severe pain on swallowing. Endoscopy shows several shallow ulcers in the distal oesophagus. A blood CMV PCR is weakly positive.
questions.leadIn: What is the best way to confirm CMV oesophagitis?
options: Biopsy of the ulcers for histology and CMV PCR
questions.explanation: In HIV, CMV reactivates in the blood intermittently and **blood CMV correlates poorly with disease**. In the immunocompromised, the diagnosis is made by showing CMV **in the affected organ**, here by **biopsy** looking for cytomegalic cells with inclusions, PCR or antigen.
whyNot: Blood CMV detection is unhelpful for diagnosis in HIV because reactivation does not match clinical disease.
Antibody tests are unreliable in the immunocompromised, and most adults are seropositive anyway.
CMV is shed in urine for life, so urine testing helps only in neonates.
The heterophile test is for EBV infectious mononucleosis.

questions.stem: A 30-year-old woman receiving chemotherapy for acute leukaemia shared a hospital bay with a patient who developed chickenpox 9 days ago. She has never had chickenpox, and her VZV IgG is negative. She has no rash.
questions.leadIn: What is the most appropriate action?
options: No action; it is too late for prophylaxis
Check VZV IgM and act on the result
Isolate her and await a rash before doing anything
questions.explanation: She meets all three VZIG criteria: significant contact, susceptibility and severe immunosuppression. VZIG is ideally given within **7 days**, but Davidson notes it **may still attenuate disease up to 10 days** after exposure. Day 9 is still worth giving. If chickenpox develops, she needs aciclovir.
whyNot: The window extends to 10 days, so it is not too late.
A live vaccine is not the post-exposure measure for a severely immunosuppressed patient.
IgM would not guide prophylaxis; susceptibility is already shown by the negative IgG.
Waiting for a rash loses the chance to attenuate a potentially fatal infection.

questions.stem: A 26-year-old woman is travelling to Indonesia for a month and asks how best to avoid dengue.
questions.leadIn: Which advice is most accurate?
options: Use insect repellent during the day, because the vector bites in daylight
Sleeping under a bed net at night gives good protection
Malaria chemoprophylaxis will also prevent dengue
Avoid contact with monkeys and poultry
questions.explanation: _Aedes aegypti_ is a **day-biting** mosquito, so **daytime repellents** matter most. Bed nets help little against it.
whyNot: Bed nets are not very effective against a mosquito that bites in the daytime.
Antimalarials have no activity against the dengue virus.
Dengue is spread by mosquito bites, not by water.
Dengue spreads between humans via Aedes; avoiding animals does not prevent it.

questions.stem: A woman develops a chickenpox rash 2 days before giving birth at term. Her baby is well at birth.
questions.leadIn: What is the most appropriate management for the baby?
options: No action, as the baby looks well
Give the baby the live varicella vaccine
Treat only the mother with aciclovir
Check the baby’s VZV IgG and act only if negative
questions.explanation: Maternal chickenpox **within 5 days before (or 2 days after) delivery** puts the newborn at risk of **severe neonatal varicella** with visceral involvement and bleeding. Davidson lists such a baby as meeting the VZIG criteria; K&C likewise protects the baby with ZIG when delivery is within 7 days of the mother’s rash.
whyNot: Looking well at birth does not exclude severe neonatal varicella developing later.
The live vaccine is given after age 1 and is not post-exposure protection for a newborn.
Treating the mother does not protect the exposed baby.
Testing delays protection; the timing of the mother’s rash alone defines the baby as at risk.

ospe.identify: Panel A: a generalised vesicular rash, heaviest on the trunk → **chickenpox** (primary VZV).
An adult with a generalised varicella rash → **adult chickenpox**; think of the risk of varicella pneumonitis, especially in smokers.
A one-sided vesicular eruption in a single dermatome → **shingles** (VZV reactivation from a sensory ganglion).
Grouped vesicles on a red base in a dermatomal band → **herpes zoster**; ask about pain before the rash and check for V1 involvement.
Panel A: atypical (reactive) lymphocytes → **infectious mononucleosis**. Panel B: widespread rash after **ampicillin** in IM.
An enlarged cell with an intranuclear **“owl’s eye” inclusion** → **cytomegalovirus** infection on histology.
